_note: Where the sim lets a route cross a river cheaply. A crossing site makes the river's crossing cost fall to cost_factor times the usual within about three miles of the site: a bridge (0.15), a ferry (0.4), a known ford (0.5). Anywhere else on the river a route pays the full cost. Dates are the dates the crossing was usable; the sim applies every site that was still usable in 1874 for the whole run (a bridge built later than 1874 is treated as built), so the dates are recorded but not yet used. Positions are from memory of the sites' places today: exact only where the site is a town.

crossings.name: Hannibal Bridge, Kansas City
crossings.what: The first permanent rail crossing of the Missouri River, opened July 3, 1869; a swing bridge designed by Octave Chanute
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Union Pacific bridge, Omaha
crossings.what: The first railroad bridge across the Missouri at Omaha, opened March 27, 1872 (a UP ferry ran from 1866); tolls through the 1870s and 1880s; wind damage in 1877
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Fort Laramie bridge
crossings.what: A 400-foot iron bridge for the Army, authorised by Congress in January 1874 ($15,000, King Bridge Company) to replace an unreliable government ferry and to serve the Cheyenne-Fort Laramie-Black Hills freight road; built 1875 (the NPS page says 1876)
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Red River Station ferry
crossings.what: Drovers crossed the Red River here from 1867 (the Abilene or Chisholm Trail); a toll chain ferry ran about half a mile west of the town

crossings.name: Doan's Crossing
crossings.what: The Western Trail's Red River crossing in Wilbarger County, used from about 1876; Andy Adams wrote that more men drowned at the Red River crossings than on all other rivers together
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Arkansas River bridge, Wichita
crossings.what: A bridge separated Wichita from the settlement of Delano by about 1870 (a photograph catalogued by the National Cowboy Museum; no builder, toll or exact date found)
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Tascosa crossing
crossings.what: A crossing of the Canadian River for centuries, named for the quicksand at the crossing; the Dodge City freight road crossed here
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Ogallala South Platte crossing
crossings.what: Texas herds reached the Union Pacific at Ogallala across the South Platte. Andy Adams's novel The Log of a Cowboy (based on his drives) has chapters 'Ogalalla', 'Swimming the Platte', 'The North Platte' and 'Forty Islands Ford'. Nothing found on where the ford was, and the UP bridged the river for the railroad

crossings.name: Dodge City Arkansas River ford
crossings.what: The Western Trail brought herds across the Arkansas to the Santa Fe at Dodge City. A Dodge City Public Library photograph of 1887 shows a bridge over the river; nothing found on an 1870s ford, ferry or toll bridge or where the herds crossed

crossings.name: Fort Benton levee and ferry
crossings.what: The head of steamboat navigation from 1860: the freight for the northwest was unloaded on its levee until a railroad arrived in 1887
crossings.position: at the town or site named

crossings.name: Miles City Yellowstone River crossing
crossings.what: Fort Keogh and Miles City stand at the junction of the Yellowstone and Tongue rivers; steamboats brought the post's construction materials up the Yellowstone (construction from 1877). Nothing found on a ferry or ford

crossings.name: Waco Suspension Bridge
crossings.what: A toll suspension bridge over the Brazos, opened November 20, 1869 per Wikipedia (January 1 or 7, 1870 per others); the Waco Bridge Company, chartered 1866, held a monopoly and allowed no other bridge within five miles for twenty-five years; before it, Chisholm Trail herds forded at Waco, one of the shallow fords; the county bought it and freed it of tolls in 1889
